topics.title: Sets
topics.summary: Set notation, Venn diagrams and counting with two sets.
notes: ## What is a set?
A **set** is a well-defined collection of objects called **elements** or **members**. Sets are named with capital letters and listed inside curly brackets.
- A = {2, 4, 6, 8} is the set of even numbers from 2 to 8.
- 4 ∈ A means "4 is an element of A"; 5 ∉ A means "5 is not an element of A".
- n(A) is the **number of elements** in A, so n(A) = 4.
## Key vocabulary
| Term | Symbol | Meaning |
| Universal set | ξ | everything under consideration |
| Empty set | ∅ or { } | a set with no elements |
| Subset | A ⊂ B | every element of A is also in B |
| Union | A ∪ B | elements in A **or** B (or both) |
| Intersection | A ∩ B | elements in **both** A and B |
| Complement | A′ | elements of ξ that are **not** in A |
## Venn diagrams
A rectangle represents the universal set and circles represent the sets inside it. The overlap of two circles is their intersection.
## Counting with two sets
> Tip: in Venn diagram problems, fill in the **intersection first**, then work outwards.
## Number of subsets
A set with n elements has 2^n subsets, including ∅ and the set itself.

examples.q: ξ = {1, 2, 3, …, 10}, A = {even numbers}, B = {multiples of 3}. List A ∩ B and A ∪ B.
examples.a:

A ∩ B = {6}, the only number in both sets.
A ∪ B = {2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10}.

examples.q: In a class of 40 students, 25 take Geography, 18 take History and 7 take both. How many take neither?
examples.a:
n(G ∪ H) = n(G) + n(H) − n(G ∩ H) = 25 + 18 − 7 = 36
Neither = 40 − 36 = 4 students.

topics.title: Indices and Standard Form
topics.summary: Laws of indices, zero, negative and fractional indices, standard form.
notes: ## Laws of indices
For any non-zero base a:
| Law | Rule | Example |
| Multiply: add the powers | a^m × a^n = a^{m+n} | 2^3 × 2^4 = 2^7 |
| Divide: subtract the powers | a^m ÷ a^n = a^{m−n} | 5^6 ÷ 5^2 = 5^4 |
| Power of a power | (a^m)^n = a^{mn} | (3^2)^3 = 3^6 |
| Zero index | a^0 = 1 | 7^0 = 1 |
| Negative index | a^{−n} = 1 ÷ a^n | 2^{−3} = 1/8 |
| Fractional index | a^{m/n} = (ⁿ√a)^m | 8^{2/3} = 4 |
> Tip: with fractional indices, take the **root first**, then the power. The numbers stay small.
## Standard form
A number is in **standard form** when it is written as
[[A × 10^n, where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer]]
- Large numbers have a positive n: 45 000 = 4.5 × 10^4
- Small numbers have a negative n: 0.0032 = 3.2 × 10^{−3}
## Calculating in standard form
- **Multiply**: multiply the A parts and **add** the powers, then adjust.
- **Divide**: divide the A parts and **subtract** the powers.
- **Add or subtract**: first write both numbers with the same power of 10.

examples.a:
Root first: ⁴√16 = 2
Then the power: 2^3 = 8
So 16^{3/4} = 8

examples.q: Calculate (3 × 10^5) × (4 × 10^{−2}), giving your answer in standard form.
examples.a:
Multiply the numbers: 3 × 4 = 12
Add the powers: 10^{5 + (−2)} = 10^3
12 × 10^3 is not in standard form because 12 ≥ 10, so write 12 = 1.2 × 10^1
Answer: 1.2 × 10^4

topics.title: Linear Equations and Inequalities
topics.summary: Solving equations, simultaneous equations and inequalities.
notes: ## Solving linear equations
An equation stays balanced if you do the **same thing to both sides**.
1. Remove brackets by expanding.
2. Collect the terms in x on one side and the numbers on the other.
3. Divide by the coefficient of x.
## Equations with fractions
Multiply every term by the **LCM of the denominators** first. For x/2 + x/3 = 5, multiply by 6: 3x + 2x = 30, so x = 6.
## Simultaneous equations
Two equations with two unknowns can be solved by:
- **Elimination**: make the coefficients of one letter equal, then add or subtract the equations.
- **Substitution**: make one letter the subject, then substitute it into the other equation.
## Linear inequalities
Solve them like equations, using <, >, ≤ or ≥.
> **Reverse the inequality sign** whenever you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number: −2x > 6 gives x < −3.
On a number line, use an **open circle** for < or > and a **closed circle** for ≤ or ≥.

examples.q: Solve the simultaneous equations 2x + y = 11 and x − y = 1.
examples.a:
Add the equations to eliminate y: 3x = 12, so x = 4
Substitute into x − y = 1: 4 − y = 1, so y = 3
Check: 2(4) + 3 = 11 ✓
Answer: x = 4, y = 3

questions.prompt: Find the largest integer x that satisfies 4x − 1 < 15.

Add to the first: 7x = 28, so x = 4  [1]

topics.title: Quadratic Equations
topics.summary: Factorisation, the quadratic formula and the discriminant.
notes: ## The general quadratic
[[ax^2 + bx + c = 0, where a ≠ 0]]
A quadratic equation has at most **two** solutions (roots).
## Method 1: Factorisation
Find two numbers that **multiply to ac** and **add to b**.
- If the product of two brackets is zero, **one of them must be zero**.
## Method 2: The quadratic formula
Use it when the quadratic does not factorise easily:
The **discriminant** b^2 − 4ac tells you how many real roots there are:
| b^2 − 4ac | Roots |
| greater than 0 | two different real roots |
| equal to 0 | one repeated root |
| less than 0 | no real roots |
## Difference of two squares

topics.title: Mensuration
topics.summary: Perimeter, area, arcs and sectors, volume and surface area.
notes: ## Perimeter and area
| Shape | Perimeter | Area |
| Rectangle | 2(l + w) | l × w |
| Triangle | sum of the sides | ½ × base × height |
| Parallelogram | sum of the sides | base × height |
| Trapezium | sum of the sides | ½(a + b) × h |
| Circle | 2πr (circumference) | πr^2 |
> Units matter: lengths are in cm or m, areas in cm^2 or m^2, and volumes in cm^3 or m^3.
## Arcs and sectors
For a sector with angle θ at the centre:
[[arc length = (θ ÷ 360) × 2πr]]
[[sector area = (θ ÷ 360) × πr^2]]
## Volume and surface area
- **Prism** (constant cross-section): volume = area of cross-section × length
- **Cylinder**: V = πr^2h, curved surface area = 2πrh
- **Cone**: V = ⅓πr^2h
- **Sphere**: V = (4/3)πr^3, surface area = 4πr^2
## Converting units

examples.q: Find the area of a trapezium whose parallel sides are 8 cm and 12 cm, and whose height is 5 cm.
A cylindrical tank has radius 0.7 m and height 2 m. Find its capacity in litres. (Take π = 22/7.)
examples.a:
V = πr^2h = 22/7 × 0.7 × 0.7 × 2 = 3.08 m^3
1 m^3 = 1000 litres
Capacity = 3080 litres

topics.title: Trigonometry
topics.summary: Pythagoras, SOH CAH TOA, angles of elevation and depression.
notes: ## Pythagoras' theorem
In a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse c (the longest side, opposite the right angle):
## The three trigonometric ratios
Label the sides relative to the angle θ: **Opposite**, **Adjacent** and **Hypotenuse**.
[[sin θ = O ÷ H      cos θ = A ÷ H      tan θ = O ÷ A]]
> Memory aid: **SOH CAH TOA**
## Finding a side or an angle
- To find a **side**, choose the ratio that links the side you know with the side you want, then rearrange.
- To find an **angle**, use the inverse function, e.g. θ = tan^{−1}(O ÷ A).
## Angles of elevation and depression
- The **angle of elevation** is measured **upwards** from the horizontal.
- The **angle of depression** is measured **downwards** from the horizontal.
- The angle of elevation from A to B equals the angle of depression from B to A (alternate angles).
## Special values

examples.q: A ladder 5 m long leans against a wall with its foot 3 m from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
examples.a:
The ladder is the hypotenuse.
h^2 + 3^2 = 5^2
h^2 = 25 − 9 = 16
h = 4 m

examples.q: From a point 50 m from the foot of a tower, the angle of elevation of the top is 32°. Find the height of the tower.
examples.a:
Opposite = height h, adjacent = 50 m, so use tan.
tan 32° = h ÷ 50
h = 50 × tan 32° = 50 × 0.6249 = 31.2 m (3 s.f.)

topics.title: Statistics
topics.summary: Mean, median, mode, range, frequency tables and pie charts.
notes: ## Types of data
- **Discrete** data can only take particular values (for example, the number of siblings).
- **Continuous** data can take any value in a range (for example, height, mass or time).
## Averages
| Measure | How to find it | Best used when |
| Mean | sum of the values ÷ number of values | there are no extreme values |
| Median | the middle value once the data is in order | there are extreme values (outliers) |
| Mode | the value that occurs most often | you want the most common value |
For n ordered values, the median is the value in position (n + 1) ÷ 2.
## Spread
[[range = highest value − lowest value]]
## Mean from a frequency table
[[mean = Σfx ÷ Σf]]
Multiply each value x by its frequency f, add up the products, then divide by the total frequency.
## Displaying data
Bar charts, pie charts, histograms and frequency polygons. In a **pie chart**, the angle for each group is (frequency ÷ total) × 360°.

topics.title: Probability
topics.summary: The probability scale, combined events and tree diagrams.
notes: ## The probability scale
Probability measures how likely an event is, from **0 (impossible)** to **1 (certain)**. It can be written as a fraction, a decimal or a percentage.
[[P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of possible outcomes]]
This works when all outcomes are equally likely.
## Complementary events
## Combined events
- **Mutually exclusive** events cannot happen together: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
- **Independent** events do not affect each other: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)
## Tree diagrams
- A **possibility space** lists every outcome; a table for two dice has 36 outcomes.
- On a **tree diagram**, multiply **along** the branches and add **between** the end results.
- **Without replacement**, the probabilities on the second set of branches change.
## Relative frequency
[[relative frequency = number of times the event happened ÷ number of trials]]
The more trials you do, the closer the relative frequency gets to the true probability.

examples.q: A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green beads. One bead is picked at random. Find P(blue) and P(not blue).
A fair coin is tossed and a fair die is rolled. Find the probability of a head and a six.
examples.a:
The events are independent.
P(head) = 1/2 and P(six) = 1/6
P(head and six) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12
